title: The growth of Swiss hydropower
place: All of Switzerland, mainly the Alps (Valais, Graubünden, Ticino, Uri, Bern) and the large rivers of the Plateau (Rhine, Aare, Rhône)
built: From about 1880 to today; main building time 1945–1970
summary: Between 1913 and 2025 the power of Swiss hydropower plants grew from about 620 MW to about 16,500 MW; hydropower now gives about 58% of Swiss electricity.
why: Switzerland has steep mountains and much rain and snow. These are ideal conditions for water power. In earlier times water drove mills and smithies; at the end of the 19th century more than 10,000 small water power plants worked. The first electric plants followed: Letten in Zurich (1878) and La Coulouvrenière in Geneva (1886) were low-pressure plants. Taulan near Montreux (1887) was the first high-pressure plant (a plant with a high fall of water).

The federal water rights law of 1916 gave the legal basis for large plants. Run-of-river plants (plants on a river without a large lake) were built on the large rivers, for example on the Rhine. Storage plants with dams were built in the Alps; they produce a large part of their power in winter. The most intensive building time was 1955 to 1970: demand grew fast, good sites were free and there was no competing technology.

After 1970 building slowed down. Reasons were the oil crisis, the new nuclear power plants and more public criticism of large projects. In the 1980s building almost stopped. Since about 1990 operators mostly renew plants and increase their power. New large projects are pumped storage plants (plants that pump water up to a lake and use it again later).
gained: In 1913 the hydropower plants had a maximum power of 624 MW and an expected production of 3,130 GWh per year. At the end of 2025 the 722 plants (16 abroad) had 16,475 MW and about 37,162 GWh per year.
Hydropower gives about 58.5% of Swiss electricity production (10-year average). In the early 1970s the share was almost 90%; nuclear power reduced it to about 60% by 1985.
Storage and pumped storage plants make electricity in winter. About 41.8% of the expected production comes in the winter half-year.
The cantons and communes receive money from the plants: water fees (Wasserzins) of about 550 million francs per year (federal figure of 2018), plus taxes and concession fees.
lost: Most of the many small water power plants of the 19th century were closed in the 20th century. In 1914 there were still about 7,000 plants up to 10 MW; large plants and engines replaced most of them.

About 1,500 water intakes for hydropower take water from rivers and streams. Below the intakes the rivers carry only residual flow (the water that is left); some streams still fall dry at times. See the change 'The fight for residual flow'.
Dams flooded high valleys, and some projects were fought hard (Urseren, Silsersee, Rheinau, Greina). In 1965 the ice fall at the Mattmark building site killed 88 workers.
About 1,000 obstacles at hydropower plants block fish migration, and about 100 plants cause hydropeaking (fast changes of flow). See the change 'Hydropeaking'.

stops.title: The first wave: electric light and river plants
text: In 1913 the statistics list 835 water power plants with 20 PS (horsepower) or more. Together they had 624 MW and an expected production of 3,130 GWh per year.
The number of electricity works grew from 140 in 1900 to more than 1,000 in 1913. Large run-of-river plants were built on the Rhine, for example at Rheinfelden and Laufenburg.

stops.title: Between the wars: large dams and river plants
text: Companies built large storage plants and river plants, often together with partner companies. Examples are the Grimsel lake with the Oberhasli plants and the Rhine plant Ryburg-Schwörstadt.
At the end of 1946 the 283 larger plants had 2,770 MW and an expected production of 10,451 GWh per year.

stops.title: The great building time
text: From 1955 to 1970 Switzerland built more hydropower than ever before. Large dams such as Grande Dixence and Göscheneralp were finished in this time (see those changes).
Between 1950 and 1970 the power grew from 2,870 MW to 9,628 MW. In the early 1970s hydropower gave almost 90% of Swiss electricity.

stops.title: Today: renewal and pumped storage
text: At the end of 2025 there were 706 plants of 300 kW or more in Switzerland. All plants together have 16,475 MW and an expected production of about 37,162 GWh per year.
About 63% of the energy comes from the mountain cantons Uri, Graubünden, Ticino and Valais. New large plants are mostly pumped storage plants, such as Limmern (2016) and Nant de Drance (2022).

notes: A text-only change with places only: no national shape can be drawn. Places are power stations from the federal WASTA statistics (layer ch.bfe.statistik-wasserkraftanlagen, state 31.12.2025), queried with geoadmin.py for all of Switzerland (727 records). The places are the largest stations by expected production or by power, plus Taulan (the first high-pressure plant named by HLS). The year in brackets is the WASTA field 'beginningofoperation'; for old plants that were rebuilt (e.g. Rheinfelden, rebuilt about 2010) WASTA still shows the first year, but this was not checked for every plant. Kembs is in France; Switzerland has a share (WASTA canton field empty). Capacity and production numbers come from the BFE table 'Entwicklung der Leistung und der mittleren Produktionserwartung 1913-2024' and the BFE note 'Stand der Wasserkraftnutzung am 31.12.2025'. These are EXPECTED average productions, not measured production; real production changes with the weather (about 30 TWh in 1996 to 42.3 TWh in 2001, BFE 2006). The counting limits changed over time (1913: plants of 20 PS or more; 1916-1972: 330 kW or more; from 1973: 300 kW or more), so the numbers of plants are not fully comparable. The HLS figures 1880-1950 (249 GWh to 12,758 GWh) are for all electricity production of private and public companies, not hydropower only, so they are not used as hydropower numbers. Map years: 1914, 1946 and 1970 are years of the BFE table close to the end of each period. Sources check: quotes re-copied from opened sources (BFE Exkurs 2006, BFE tables 1913–2024 and 31.12.2025, VSA D11, HLS Stauwerke and Elektrizitätswirtschaft via web.archive.org, BAFU Restwasser page, BAFU report 2024, WASTA, DHS Grande Dixence). Changes: 'mills and workshops' -> 'mills and smithies' (BFE); 'from the 1880s plants for electric light' replaced by HLS facts (Letten 1878, Coulouvrenière 1886); 'keep summer water for the winter' replaced by BFE winter share figures; Mauvoisin removed from story stop 3 (no opened source; Göscheneralp 1962 from HLS). Note: BFE table 2024 gives 16,576 MW, the 2025 note 16,475 MW; text uses 2025.

title: Mittelbünden power plants of the city of Zurich (ewz): Julia and Albula
place: Surses (Oberhalbstein) and the Albula valley, from Marmorera to Tiefencastel, Sils im Domleschg and Rothenbrunnen
summary: The city of Zurich uses the Julia and the Albula in several steps, from the Marmorera reservoir through Tinizong and Tiefencastel to Sils and Rothenbrunnen; the rivers keep only residual flow between the intakes and the stations.
why: The electricity works of the city of Zurich (ewz) built a first station on the Albula at Sils im Domleschg in 1910. In 1944 ewz got the water rights for the Julia below Cunter. From 1946 to 1948 it built the Tiefencastel West station. A weir at Burvagn holds back the Julia. After the turbines the water goes into the Albula.

From 1950 to 1954 ewz built the Marmorera dam (see the change Marmorera). Its water drives the Tinizong station. The HLS says it runs since 1953; the federal list gives 1954. Later stations followed at Tiefencastel Ost (1970) and Rothenbrunnen (1976). Water taken from the Albula at Solis goes to Sils and to Rothenbrunnen.

For a long time the Julia below the Marmorera dam got no residual flow. In December 2016 the canton set new residual flows after a round table. Since 2020 more water flows from the Marmorera dam into the Julia. Since 2026 a small station at Burvagn uses the residual flow there.
gained: The federal statistics list Tinizong (1954, 69.5 MW, 202 GWh per year) and Tiefencastel Ost (1970, 52 MW, 151 GWh). They also list Tiefencastel West (1949, 24 MW, 47 GWh), Sils (1910, 26 MW, 117 GWh) and Rothenbrunnen (1976, 44 MW, 186 GWh).
The new concession of Tiefencastel West was signed in December 2021 and runs to 2050. For it ewz pays 12.5 million francs to the communes Surses and Albula/Alvra and to the canton.
The 2016 solution also pays for the improvement of the fens (flat moors) on the Alp Flix.
lost: On the 2007 BAFU sheets the Julia had zero residual flow below the Marmorera dam and below the Burvagn weir.
At Solis the Albula keeps 0.36 to 0.57 m³/s. Its natural flow there is about 5 to 40 m³/s (BAFU sheet of 2007). The Albula gorge between Solis and Sils loses most of its water.

More residual flow in the Julia costs production: the Marmorera residual water can no longer be used at Tinizong (about 25 GWh per year). In all ewz plants in Graubünden the loss is about 46 GWh per year.
The water returned at Sils and Rothenbrunnen causes hydropeaking (fast changes of flow) in the Hinterrhein.

title: Ticino river power stations in the Leventina
place: Leventina, the Ticino valley from Airolo to Personico
summary: Three run-of-river steps take the Ticino out of its bed between Airolo and Personico; today the canton's company AET runs them.
why: The Biaschina station near Bodio started in 1911. Its cheap power brought factories to Bodio.
The Piottino station at Lavorgo started on 1 May 1932. It uses the Ticino from Rodi, where a small basin was built in 1940. The Stalvedro station (1968) at Piotta uses the Ticino below Airolo.

A cantonal law of 25 June 1958 created AET (Azienda elettrica ticinese) so that the canton could run its own plants. In December 1958 parliament gave it Biaschina and Tremorgio. AET built the Nuova Biaschina (1966, between Lavorgo and Personico) and took over Piottino after the canton bought it back in 1972.
gained: Piottino produced about 300 million kWh (300 GWh) in an average year, 40 percent of it in winter (1967). The federal list today gives 69 MW and 289 GWh.
The Nuova Biaschina has 147 MW and produces about 382 GWh per year; Stalvedro 14 MW and 55 GWh.
From 1911 the cheap electricity of the Biaschina and the railway made Bodio the most important industrial place of the canton, says the historical dictionary (HLS/DSS).
With AET the canton runs these plants itself. The Ticino parliament decided this for Biaschina and Tremorgio in December 1958.
lost: The Ticino keeps only residual flows: 350 to 650 l/s at Airolo, 300 to 500 l/s at Rodi and 100 l/s at Lavorgo. At Airolo the winter minimum is 795 l/s since the decision of 2015. At Rodi the Q347 (a low flow reached 347 days a year) is 4020 l/s.
Below the sewage plant of Airolo there is too little water to dilute the cleaned waste water, says the canton.
The Ticino from Giornico to Arbedo is a home of the grayling. The canton sees a public interest in more water there.

title: Ritom railway power scheme (SBB, Ritom SA)
place: Piora plateau above Piotta, Leventina
summary: The Ritom lake and intakes on the Garegna and the Reno di Medel feed the railway power station at Piotta; La Foss below the dam lost its water until new rules came in 2015.
why: The Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) needed electricity for the Gotthard line. They dammed Lago Ritom (see that change) and built the Piotta station, which runs since 1920.
Intakes on the Garegna and the Reno di Medel bring more water into the lake. The lake water drops about 835 m in a pressure pipe to Piotta.

For a long time these intakes had to release no water. In 2015 the canton gave a new concession to Ritom SA. It set residual flows at the Foss, Garegna and Reno di Medel intakes that follow the federal law. A new pumped-storage station is being built at Piotta.
gained: The old Piotta station (Ritom 1) has 33 MW and produces about 160 GWh per year, mainly for the railway.
The new station (Ritom 2) will have 120 MW and 60 MW of pumps. The federal list expects 144 GWh per year from 2027.
The lake holds 48 million m³. About 25 percent of the output goes to the canton's company AET, which alone uses the new pump.
lost: La Foss, the outlet of Lago Ritom, lost its water below the dam. The official sheet for the Foss intake (made before the new concession) gives no residual flow.
Until the new concession of 2015 the railway intakes released no water at all, says the canton.

title: Water fees: what the mountains earn from hydropower
place: All of Switzerland; most money goes to Valais, Graubünden, Ticino, Uri, Bern and Aargau
built: Federal maximum since 1918; 110 francs per kW since 2015
summary: Hydropower operators pay a yearly water fee (Wasserzins) to the canton or commune that owns the water; today this is about 550 million francs per year, a large income for mountain regions.
why: In Switzerland the cantons own the water. Cantonal law decides if the canton, a district, a commune or a corporation can use the water power. They can use it themselves or give a licence (concession) to a company for at most 80 years. In return the company pays a yearly water fee (Wasserzins).

The federal water rights law of 1916 sets only a maximum fee. In 1918 the maximum was 6 francs per gross horsepower, about 8.16 francs per kW. Parliament revised it six times, the last time to 100 francs per kW in 2011 and 110 francs per kW in 2015. In 2018 the Federal Council proposed to keep 110 francs until the end of 2024. A fact sheet of 2022 says that the present rule applies until the end of 2030.

The fee is one reason why the mountain cantons defend hydropower. Before the vote of 1992 on stricter water protection, power producers and mountain cantons fought the initiative. They feared losing income from concessions and jobs.
gained: The cantons and communes receive about 550 million francs of water fees per year. Most of it goes to Valais, Graubünden, Ticino and Uri, and to Bern and Aargau.
In Graubünden, Uri and Valais the water fees are 13 to 23% of the tax income (with regalia and concessions). In some communes of Graubünden and Valais the share is much higher.
Graubünden shares the water fees half and half with the communes. In Valais the communes get 40% of the fees from the side rivers. On average more than 70% goes to the cantons.
The Federal Council says the money helps mountain communes to offer good, low-tax housing and to stop people from leaving. Some cantons, such as Bern and Valais, use part of it for river restoration.
lost: The fee pays for water that is then missing in the rivers below the intakes. See the change 'The fight for residual flow'.

Communes that protect a landscape and give up a power plant lose this income. Since 1992 the Confederation can pay compensation in such cases. This was used for the Greina plateau, where a reservoir plan was given up in 1986.
For the operators the fee is a cost. From 2000 to 2016 it was about 1 cent per kWh, about 20% of the production cost. Since 2015 it is about 1.5 cent per kWh.

title: Reuss railway power scheme (Pfaffensprung, Wassen, Amsteg)
place: Reuss valley between Göschenen and Amsteg
built: until 1922 (Pfaffensprung dam and Amsteg station); 1949 (Wassen stage)
summary: The Swiss Federal Railways dammed the Reuss at the Pfaffensprung and built the Amsteg station for railway power; a second stage from Göschenen to Wassen followed in 1949, so the Reuss between Göschenen and Amsteg keeps only a residual flow.
why: The Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) built their own power stations to supply electricity for their trains: Piotta with the Ritom lake in 1920 (see the change on the Lago Ritom) and Amsteg in 1922, with a weir on the Reuss at the Pfaffensprung near Wassen. The federal list gives 1923 as the start of Amsteg.

From the Pfaffensprung a tunnel leads the Reuss to the Amsteg station, 284 m lower. In 1949 a second stage started: intakes at Göschenen take the Reuss and its side streams and lead them to a station at the Pfaffensprung. The Göschenen plant of 1962 also sends railway power to Amsteg.
In 1998 two small stations were added: one at the Pfaffensprung uses the residual flow, one at Amsteg is a regulating station. The water rights end in 2043.
gained: The Amsteg station has a maximum power of 120 MW and an expected production of 443.5 GWh per year. The Wassen station at the Pfaffensprung adds 58 MW and 290 GWh.
The SBB got their own power station for railway electricity in the Reuss valley. Railway power from the Göschenen plant is also fed in at Amsteg.
lost: At the Pfaffensprung the Reuss keeps 1.2 m³/s in winter and up to 3.5 m³/s in summer. The flow above the intake is about 8 to 43 m³/s (monthly means).
At the Göschenen intake on the Reuss and on the Meienreuss and the Rohrbach no minimum flow is released (0 l/s). The Reuss below Göschenen gets mainly side streams.
Side streams at Amsteg also lose water: the Fellibach keeps 100 l/s and the Chärstelenbach 300 l/s.

title: Wägital hydropower scheme (Rempen and Siebnen)
place: Wägital, from the Wägitalersee via Rempen to Siebnen (March district)
built: until 1926 (dam finished 1924; both stations in operation 1926)
length_km: c. 10 (dry stretch of the Wägitaler Aa)
summary: The Wägital scheme leads the water of the Wägitalersee through two pressure tunnels to the stations Rempen and Siebnen, so the Wägitaler Aa below the dam lost most of its water.
why: People discussed a power station in the Wägital from the late 19th century. In 1909 the city of Zurich bought the spa hotel of Innerthal, also to secure the water. The Schräh dam was finished in 1924 and flooded the old village (see the change on the Wägitalersee). At 112 m it was then the highest dam in the world.

The company AG Kraftwerk Wägital uses the lake as a store. A first stage leads the water to the station Rempen. A second stage takes it again at Rempen and leads it to the station Siebnen at the mouth of the valley. Rempen can also pump water back up. Axpo and the electricity works of the city of Zurich (EWZ) run the plant.

The concession (right to use the water) ends in 2040, says the canton; the older federal sheets give 2041. The renewal started in 2025. By the end of 2030 the law asks the plant to reduce strong flow changes, to improve the river bed and to let fish migrate freely again.
gained: The station Rempen (1926) has a maximum turbine power of 66.2 MW and an expected production of 60 GWh per year. Its pumps (16 MW) can lift water back into the Wägitalersee.
The station Siebnen (1926) has 51.5 MW and an expected production of 63 GWh per year from the same water.
lost: The official intake sheets show that no minimum flow is released at the Wägitalersee and at the Rempen intake (0 l/s). The sheet for the lake also notes no overflows into the Aa. From the dam to Siebnen the Wägitaler Aa gets mainly water from side streams.
Below the station Siebnen the plant causes strong changes of flow (hydropeaking). The law asks that these be reduced by the end of 2030.
The dams and intakes block fish. The law asks that free fish migration be restored by the end of 2030.

title: Oberhasli hydropower scheme (Grimsel, Handeck, Innertkirchen)
place: Upper Aare valley (Haslital) and Gadmental, from the Grimsel Pass to Innertkirchen
summary: Kraftwerke Oberhasli (KWO) collect the water of the upper Aare and the Gadmental in reservoirs and tunnels and send it through a chain of power stations down to Innertkirchen.
why: The Bernese power company BKW got the right to use the water of the upper Aare in 1906. In 1925 a cantonal vote in Bern approved a loan of 12 million francs, and the company Kraftwerke Oberhasli (KWO) was founded on 20 June 1925.

The first stage (1925–1932) dammed the Grimselsee and the Gelmersee (see the change on the Grimselsee) and built the Handeck 1 station. Later stages added the Oberaarsee (see that change), more stations at Handeck, Innertkirchen, Hopflauenen and Fuhren, and the pumped storage station Grimsel 2 (it pumps water up when power is cheap and makes power when it is needed).

The water now runs in tunnels instead of in the Aare. Plans to make the Grimselsee much larger (Grimsel West) caused a long political conflict in the 1980s and 1990s, and KWO dropped them in 2000. The concessions (rights to use the water) end in 2042; strict residual flow rules from the 1992 water protection law apply at renewal.
gained: The 15 stations of the scheme in the federal list (WASTA) have together a maximum turbine power of about 1320 MW and an expected production of about 1790 GWh per year (our sum of the list). The largest is Innertkirchen 1 with 394 MW and 768 GWh.
Grimsel 2 (1981) is a pumped storage station: 388 MW in turbine mode and 347 MW in pump mode. It moves water between the Grimselsee and the Oberaarsee to store energy.
The HLS calls the Kraftwerke Oberhasli an important employer for the Oberhasli region.
lost: Below the Räterichsboden dam and again at Handeck, the official intake sheets show that all the inflow of the Aare is taken and no minimum flow is released (0 l/s). The Aare gorge down to Innertkirchen gets only side streams and spill water.
The Triftwasser intake takes all its inflow (0 l/s released). At its intake the Gadmerwasser keeps only 25 l/s in winter and 50 l/s in summer.
Below Innertkirchen the stations release their water in fast surges (hydropeaking). Before a basin was built to slow them down, fish were often stranded and the number of insects was below average.

title: Etzelwerk (Sihlsee to Altendorf, railway power)
place: From the Sihlsee near Einsiedeln through the Etzel ridge to Altendorf on Lake Zurich
length_km: c. 6.4 (dry stretch of the Sihl to the Alp)
summary: The Etzelwerk takes the water of the upper Sihl from the Sihlsee through the Etzel ridge to a power station on Lake Zurich, so the Sihl below the dam keeps only a residual flow.
why: The upper Sihl flows north, away from Lake Zurich, but Lake Zurich lies much lower on the other side of the Etzel ridge. The fall height (difference in height used by the turbines) is 475 m, says the federal list. The concession (right to use the water) was negotiated in the 1920s between the cantons of Zurich, Schwyz and Zug, the districts of Einsiedeln and Höfe, and the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB).

The SBB built the dam in den Schlagen, the Hüendermatt dam, a pressure line to Altendorf, the power station and an outlet canal to Lake Zurich. The Etzelwerk started on 12 May 1937. The Sihlsee itself is a separate change (see Sihlsee).

After 50 years the parties went to court about the future of the concession. The Federal Supreme Court decided in 1988 that the old concession ends on 12 May 2017. After a transition period, a new concession for 80 years started on 1 January 2023. It asks for much higher residual flows.
gained: The Etzelwerk station at Altendorf has a maximum turbine power of 140 MW and an expected production of about 241 GWh per year. Its pumps (54 MW) can also lift water from Lake Zurich back into the Sihlsee.
The Etzelwerk belongs to the SBB and makes electricity for the railways.
The reservoir dampens flood peaks on the Sihl. It also keeps the river bed from drying out in winter.
lost: Under the old concession only 300 l/s (winter) to 400 l/s (summer) were released into the Sihl below the dam. Natural monthly mean flows there are about 3.4 to 15 m³/s.
The water of the upper Sihl goes to Lake Zurich instead of down the Sihl. The HLS says that the lower flow makes the water quality of the Sihl worse.
Fewer high flows can let the river bed clog with fine material. The 2023 concession therefore asks for at least two high flows of up to 200 m³/s in ten years below the mouth of the Alp.

title: Lucendro scheme: Reuss water to the Ticino
place: Gotthard pass area, Airolo (TI) and the upper Gotthardreuss towards Hospental (UR)
summary: The Lucendro and Sella reservoirs on the Gotthard send water that once flowed north into the Reuss to the Airolo station on the Ticino.
why: In 1942 the cantons of Ticino and Uri gave water rights to Aare-Tessin AG (Atel). It built the Lucendro dam (1942–1945) and the Sella dam (1945–1948). The station at Airolo ran partly from 1945.

The Lucendro lake lies in Ticino, but its water naturally flows north into the Gotthardreuss and the canton of Uri. A 4.8 km pressure tunnel takes it under the watershed to Airolo. The water drops about 900 to 1,000 m (the sources give 900 m, 977 m and 996 m) and goes into the Ticino.

Because the water comes from two cantons, two concessions were needed. The cantons count 55 percent of the water as from Uri and 45 percent from Ticino. In 2024 the two cantons agreed to own the plant half each.
gained: The plant has 60 MW and produces about 100 GWh in an average year, about 68 percent of it in winter.
The two reservoirs store about 25 million m³ (Lucendro) and 9 million m³ (Sella) of water.

In 2024 Uri and Ticino agreed that each will hold 50 percent of the plant from 1 January 2025, under a new concession of 60 years. The details still had to go to the two cantonal parliaments; until the new rule comes into force, Lucendro AG runs the plant. Whether it is in force today is not confirmed.
lost: The water of the Lucendro catchment (16.7 km²) no longer flows north into the Reuss valley of Uri. It is taken under the watershed to the Ticino.
The official sheet for the Reuss intake below the dam gives no residual flow. In winter the bottom outlets of three intakes must stay fully open, says the canton.
The map of 1941 shows the natural Lago di Lucendro. A dam of 68.5 m turned it into a reservoir.

title: Maggia hydropower scheme (Ofima)
place: Valle Maggia, Val Bavona, Val Bedretto and Centovalli, down to Lago Maggiore
summary: Reservoirs, tunnels and five power stations take most of the water of the Maggia and the Bavona to Lago Maggiore at Verbano.
why: Ofima (Officine Idroelettriche della Maggia) was founded on 10 December 1949, after the Ticino parliament gave the water rights of the Maggia in March 1949.

In the first stage (Maggia I, from Sambuco to Verbano) Ofima built the Sambuco dam and the Peccia, Cavergno and Verbano power stations. Verbano started in March 1953, Peccia in September 1953 and Cavergno in June 1955. The second stage (Maggia II, concession of 1962) added the Naret and Cavagnoli lakes, Robiei and the Bavona station. A tunnel also brings water from the Val Bedretto (Ticino basin) into the Maggia system.

In spring 1954 the Maggia fell dry for the first time below the intakes. This started a debate about minimum flows (the least water that must stay in a river) that is still open. The concessions run 80 years: to 2035 (Maggia I) and 2048 (Maggia II). The canton wants to run the plants itself through its company AET.
gained: Ofima's plants have 600 MW of installed power and produce on average 1265 GWh per year (Ofima). The federal list gives for example Cavergno 108 MW and 376 GWh, Verbano 1 104 MW and 346 GWh.
Robiei and Peccia are pumped-storage stations (pumped storage means water can also be pumped back up). Robiei has 192 MW of turbines and 140 MW of pumps.
On the building sites of Maggia I about 1700 workers were employed on average from 1950 to 1956. The maximum was 2428 workers in summer 1953.

When the concessions end, the dams and tunnels go back to the canton without payment; the machines must be paid for. In 2021 the government and a committee of the Ticino parliament proposed to refuse Ofima's request to renew the concession and to run the plants through AET. The final vote of parliament was not checked.
lost: When the gates closed in spring 1954, the bed of the Maggia was dry. The writer Plinio Martini described a dry riverbed and a muddy pool under the bridge of Bignasco.

Today the official sheets give no residual flow at the upper Maggia intake (Sambuco) and 50 to 100 l/s at the Maggia intake for the Peccia station. Above that intake the river carries between 0.19 and 3.26 m³/s, depending on the month. At Bignasco 1200 to 1800 l/s must stay in the river (rule of 1982).

The canton sees the Maggia from Bignasco to Losone as a home of the grayling (a fish on the Swiss red list). In 2018 it ordered higher flows. In April 2022 the cantonal administrative court annulled the order, and the canton suspended the procedure.
Water of the Ticino from the Val Bedretto no longer flows down the Leventina. It is led through a tunnel to Robiei and the Maggia valley.

title: Grande Dixence network: glacier water from Zermatt to Arolla
place: Val d'Hérémence, Val d'Hérens (Arolla, Ferpècle), Mattertal (Zermatt), Val de Nendaz and the Rhône valley at Riddes
built: 1951–1965 (main network); 1993–1998 (Cleuson-Dixence and Bieudron); repaired 2005–2009 after the accident of 2000
summary: About 100 km of tunnels collect glacier water from 75 intakes between Zermatt and Arolla for the Lac des Dix; four power stations use it on its way to the Rhône.
why: In winter the mountain rivers carry little water. A large reservoir can store summer meltwater for the winter. Grande Dixence SA was founded in 1950 to build a much larger scheme than the first Dixence dam of 1929–1935 (see the change 'Grande Dixence').

The Val des Dix alone does not give enough water. So the company built collection tunnels (tunnels that gather water from many streams) to the glaciers of the Val d'Hérens and of the Mattertal near Zermatt. Pumping stations at Z'Mutt, Stafel, Ferpècle and Arolla lift water into a main tunnel 24 km long at about 2,400 m. From the lake, the water falls through the stations of Fionnay and Nendaz, and also Chandoline.

The Cleuson-Dixence project added a new pressure shaft (a steel-lined tunnel that carries water under high pressure) and the underground Bieudron station near Riddes. Grande Dixence SA gives 1993–1998 for the works; Alpiq gives 1993–2000. On 12 December 2000 the shaft burst above the Rhône valley. Bieudron stood still for nine years and ran again from January 2010.
gained: The scheme makes about 2,000 GWh (2 billion kWh) of electricity per year on average. Grande Dixence SA says the water is collected from 420 km², of which about two thirds are glaciers; the HLS gives a basin of 600 km².
The federal plant statistics list Bieudron with 1,269 MW (from 1999), Nendaz with 392 MW (from 1960) and Fionnay with 306 MW (from 1957).
The network brings about 500 million m³ of water per year to the Lac des Dix, where it can be stored from summer to winter.
lost: Many intakes take all the water. On the federal residual flow sheets for the Borgne de Ferpècle and the Borgne d'Arolla, the water taken is the same as the flow above the intake in every month.
Below the dam, the Dixence gets no prescribed release: the official sheets give 0 l/s for every month.
On 12 December 2000 the pressure shaft burst. About 50,000 m³ of water and mud flowed down the slope. Three people died, and two chalets and farm buildings were swept away.
Glacier water of the Mattertal is pumped over into another valley. The official sheet for the Z'Mutt intake shows all the flow taken in every month.

stops.title: Residual flow and the end of the concessions
text: The official sheets for most intakes give no release: almost all the glacier water goes into the tunnels.
The federal water protection law of 1992 sets minimum residual flows. The canton says concessions granted before 1992 must meet these rules only when they are renewed.

The official sheets give 2045 as the end of the water rights for the main intakes. When a concession ends, the communes that own the water decide on the 'droit de retour' (right of return). The wet parts of the plant (dams, tunnels, pipes) return to them free of charge.

title: Mauvoisin network: from the Val de Bagnes to Riddes
place: Val de Bagnes (Mauvoisin, Fionnay, Le Châble) and the Rhône valley at Riddes
summary: The water of the upper Val de Bagnes falls from the Lac de Mauvoisin to Fionnay and then through the mountain to Riddes; the Dranse de Bagnes below the dam carries only residual flow.
why: A high arch dam was built in the upper Val de Bagnes (see the change 'Mauvoisin'). The museum of Bagnes says more than 1,800 men worked on the site every day between 1948 and 1958.

From the lake, the water goes down to the Fionnay station (1958). Side streams such as the Torrent de Corbassière are also caught. From Fionnay a second tunnel carries water under the mountains to Riddes in the Rhône valley (1956). The small Chanrion station (1964) is also part of the network.
The upper valley has a history of floods from the Giétro glacier (see the change 'Mauvoisin'). The historical dictionary (HLS/DHS) says the dam of 1958 ended these floods.
gained: The federal plant statistics list Riddes with 271 MW and 714 GWh per year, Fionnay (Mauvoisin) with 138.6 MW and 295 GWh, and Chanrion with 33.4 MW and 80.5 GWh.
The historical dictionary (HLS/DHS) says that, besides electricity, the dam of 1958 ended the catastrophic floods caused by the Giétro glacier.
The building site gave work to more than 1,800 men every day between 1948 and 1958.
lost: At the dam, the official sheet shows that all the water is taken: the flow taken equals the flow above the intake in every month.
At Fionnay, the official sheet gives a release of only 100 l/s in winter up to 900 l/s in July. The natural low flow (Q347) there is 468 l/s. The rest goes to Riddes.

title: The fight for residual flow in Swiss rivers
place: All of Switzerland: river stretches below about 1,500 water intakes for hydropower
built: Protest from the 1950s; constitution article 1975; water protection law 1991, in force 1 November 1992; remediation deadline end of 2012
summary: After decades of conflict, the water protection law of 1991 (in force 1992) requires that rivers below hydropower intakes keep a minimum residual flow; more than half of the cantons missed the 2012 deadline to remediate old intakes.
why: Many hydropower plants take water from a river at an intake and lead it through tunnels to a power station far away. Below the intake the river keeps only the residual flow (Restwasser: the water that is left). Before 1992 there was no general federal rule, and many streams fell dry. In the 1950s the fight over the Rheinau plant on the Rhine was the first hard environmental conflict decided by a federal vote. In 1954 the voters rejected the Rheinau initiative with 68.8% no, and the plant started in 1956.

In 1975 voters added a water article to the federal constitution. It gave the Confederation the power to make rules on 'adequate residual flows'. In 1983 about 40 new hydropower projects were planned. In 1984 the fishing association and eight environmental groups handed in the initiative 'to save our waters'. Parliament answered with a new water protection law as a counter-proposal (indirect counter-proposal). On 17 May 1992 the voters rejected the initiative and accepted the law with 66.1% yes. The law came into force on 1 November 1992.

The law sets a minimum residual flow for new and renewed licences. It depends on Q347 (the flow that a river reaches or exceeds on 347 days of a year). Old intakes had to be improved (remediated) where this was possible without compensation. The first deadline was 2007; parliament moved it to the end of 2012. More than half of the cantons missed it. At the end of 2020, 934 of 1,028 intakes that needed remediation were done (91%).
gained: Rivers below intakes must keep water again. By the end of 2020, 934 intakes for hydropower were remediated, 91% of the 1,028 intakes that needed it.
In 2002 a federal study checked 8 residual flow stretches. It found that the rules can secure many organisms and the river as a habitat. Some deficits remained.
The constitution (Art. 76 of today's constitution) protects 'adequate residual flows', and every new or renewed licence must apply the law in full.
lost: Water left in the river cannot make electricity. For 107 plants with new licences, the residual flow rules cost about 318 GWh per year, about 7.6% of their possible production.
The law came slowly. Most old licences end between 2025 and 2050. Until then many stretches keep only the remediated flow. Some streams still fall dry at times.
Before the law, many streams below intakes carried little or no water for decades. The BAFU sheet of 2007 for the Dranse de Bagnes below Mauvoisin shows no residual flow at all.

stops.title: Rheinau: the first big fight
text: In 1952 building began on a power plant at the Rhine loop of Rheinau. A broad protest movement grew. In 1953 opponents handed in the Rheinau initiative, which asked to stop the works.
In 1954 the voters clearly rejected the initiative (31.2% yes). Since 1956 the plant takes up to 400 m³/s of Rhine water. The loop gets only part of the water (see the change 'Rheinau').

title: Lienne network: Tseuzier, Croix and St-Léonard
place: Valley of the Lienne (Liène) between the Rawil, Ayent and St-Léonard
summary: The water of the Tseuzier lake falls in two steps, through the cavern station of Croix and the St-Léonard station, to the Rhône.
why: Before the scheme, only the lower Lienne was used, between 911 m and 542 m. Two small plants of the town of Sion (1907 and 1917) made 27 million kWh per year. From 1945, studies showed that a reservoir at the alp of Zeuzier (Tseuzier) and two steps down to the Rhône were possible. Electricité de la Lienne SA was founded in Sion on 23 June 1953.

Works began in spring 1953 with a new road from Ayent to Zeuzier. The dam (see the change 'Tseuzier') stores 50 million m³. The upper step goes to the cavern station of Croix (head 854 m). A compensation basin at Croix then feeds the St-Léonard station (head 417 m), which returns the water to the Rhône. St-Léonard started on 16 August 1956; Croix was due to start in January 1957.
A small station at Chamarin takes water from the shaft in summer and gives it to the bisse d'Ayent (an old irrigation channel).
gained: In 1956 the planners expected 180 million kWh per year, 85% of it in winter.
The federal statistics list Croix with 66 MW and 146.5 GWh (from 1957) and St-Léonard with 36 MW and 99 GWh (from 1956).
The water from Chamarin let the owners close 4.1 km of the bisse d'Ayent, which had high upkeep costs and lost much water.
lost: Below the dam, the Lienne has a natural low flow (Q347) of only 10 l/s, and the official sheet lists no release.
One of the two old plants of Sion was closed for good in 1956, and the other ran at reduced power.
A 4.1 km stretch of the old bisse d'Ayent was taken out of service.

title: Zervreila power plants (KWZ): Vals, Safien and Rothenbrunnen
place: Vals valley, Safien valley and Domleschg (Rothenbrunnen)
summary: Water from the Zervreila reservoir in the Vals valley flows through tunnels into the Safien valley and on to Rothenbrunnen; the official sheets list no releases at the KWZ intakes on the Valser Rhein and the Rabiusa.
why: The Vals valley has a high side valley at Zervreila. The Kraftwerke Zervreila company (KWZ), based in Vals, was founded on 17 May 1952 as a partner company of electricity firms. Its aim was to store summer water for winter.

From 1953 to 1958 it built the Zervreila dam (see the change Zervreilasee), tunnels and three power stations (the HLS gives 1951–1958). Up to 1500 people worked on the sites. The water goes from the Zervreila lake through a tunnel to the Safien valley. There it collects more water from the Rabiusa at the Wanna basin and drives the Safien Platz station. A second tunnel takes the water on to the Rothenbrunnen station in the Domleschg, where it goes into the Hinterrhein.

So the water of the upper Vals valley no longer reaches the Glenner and the Vorderrhein; it reaches the Hinterrhein instead. The water rights end in 2037. KWZ now plans to raise the dam by 10 m. It also plans a 13 km tunnel to bring water from the Lugnez valley.
gained: The federal statistics list Zervreila (1958, 22.5 MW), Safien Platz (1957, 86 MW, 160 GWh per year) and Rothenbrunnen (1958, 126 MW, 327 GWh per year). KWZ gives a maximum power of 258 MW and an average of about 516 GWh per year to its partners.
The concession communes get about 30 GWh of electricity per year. Since 2008 the 22 communes and the canton own 28 percent of the company.
The works cost about 285 million francs. Much of this money went to the Swiss building and machine industry, and local firms got many orders.
lost: Below the Zervreila dam the Valser Rhein loses the water of its upper valley. At the dam the natural flow is about 0.3 m³/s in winter and up to 8.7 m³/s in summer. These numbers are from the BAFU sheet of 2007.

KWZ takes the Rabiusa in the Safien valley at Wanna (for Safien Platz) and at Safien Platz (for Rothenbrunnen). The official sheets list no release. Lower down, at Egschi, another plant (Realta) takes the Rabiusa again.
The water from the Rothenbrunnen stations causes hydropeaking (fast changes of flow) in the Hinterrhein below Rothenbrunnen.
The lake drowned the hamlets of Under and Ober Boda (see the change Zervreilasee).

title: Gougra network: Val d'Anniviers and the Turtmann valley
place: Val d'Anniviers (Moiry, Mottec, Vissoie), Turtmanntal and Chippis
summary: Three power stations in steps (Mottec, Vissoie, Chippis) use the water of the Lac de Moiry, the Navisence and a glacier stream of the Turtmann valley.
why: Alpiq, a shareholder, says the Moiry dam was built in 1954 above Grimentz (see the change 'Moiry'). The plant was put into service in 1958.

The scheme also uses water from the Turtmann valley. A small dam (30 m high) at 2,177 m catches the Turtmann glacier stream. The water falls in three steps: Moiry to Mottec, Mottec to Vissoie, and Vissoie to the Navizence station at Chippis, through tunnels of 3.4, 6.9 and 8.5 km.
The lower Navisence was used earlier: the federal statistics list the Navizence station at Chippis from 1908. The Turtmann plant at the valley exit dates from 1925.
gained: The scheme has 168 MW and produces on average 643 GWh per year.
The federal statistics list Mottec with 102 MW and pumps of 87 MW, Vissoie with 57 MW and 213 GWh, and the Navizence station at Chippis with 71.1 MW and 298.7 GWh.
lost: At the dam, the Gougra gets no prescribed release on the official sheet. Its natural low flow (Q347) is 0 l/s there.
The official sheet VS-108 for the Navisence intake (for the Vissoie power station) shows up to 11.9 m³/s taken in July. Its line for the water released is empty.
Water of the Turtmann glacier now goes to another valley. The official sheet for the Turtmannbach intake lists no release.

stops.title: Residual flow and the end of the concessions
text: The official sheets of the main intakes have an empty line for the water released. This may mean no release, or missing data (the sheets date from about 2007).
The federal water protection law of 1992 sets minimum residual flows. The canton says concessions granted before 1992 must meet these rules only when they are renewed.

The official sheets give 2039 as the end of the water rights. When a concession ends, the communes that own the water decide on the 'droit de retour' (right of return). The wet parts of the plant (dams, tunnels, pipes) return to them free of charge.

title: Göschenen hydropower scheme (Göscheneralp, Urseren, Schöllenen)
place: Göschenen valley, Urseren valley (Realp, Hospental, Andermatt) and the Schöllenen gorge
summary: The Kraftwerk Göschenen collects the Göschener Reuss in the Göscheneralpsee, adds water from the Urseren valley by tunnel, and takes the Reuss above the Schöllenen gorge, all for one station at Göschenen.
why: The power companies first wanted a very large reservoir in the Urseren valley. That plan failed. The Kraftwerk Göschenen AG was founded in Altdorf on 16 February 1955 as a replacement, to use the Göschener Reuss, the Gotthard Reuss and their side streams above Göschenen.

From 1955 to 1962 the company built the Göscheneralp dam (see the change on the Göscheneralpsee). Two tunnels of 3.9 km and 7.2 km bring water from the Voralp valley and from the upper Urseren valley into the lake. A 7.2 km pressure tunnel and a 1000 m shaft lead to an underground station at Göschenen. A second stage takes the Reuss at Andermatt, above the Schöllenen gorge.
The scheme was built jointly by the Swiss Federal Railways (SBB) and the Centralschweizerische Kraftwerke (CKW). Each partner gets half of the energy. The water rights end in 2043.
gained: In 1963 the plant was expected to make 320 GWh per year, 137 GWh of it in winter. Today WASTA lists the Göscheneralp stage with 164.8 MW and 293.3 GWh, and the Andermatt stage with 33.3 MW and 126 GWh per year.

Half of the electricity feeds the railway network through lines to Amsteg, Rupperswil and Göschenen. The CKW half went by a 225 kV line to the distribution centres of Mettlen and Rathausen (state of 1963).
lost: Below the Göscheneralp dam and at the Furkareuss intake near Realp, the official sheets show no minimum flow (0 l/s): all the inflow is taken.
At Andermatt the Reuss is taken above the Schöllenen gorge. In winter no water is released; from May to September 0.5 to 1.5 m³/s stay in the river, while the natural summer flow is 8 to 19 m³/s.

title: Bergell power plants of the city of Zurich (ewz): Albigna, Löbbia and Castasegna
place: Val Bregaglia (Bergell), from Maloja and the Albigna valley down to Castasegna on the Italian border
summary: The electricity works of the city of Zurich dammed the Albigna valley and lead the water of the Maira through tunnels from Löbbia to Castasegna; the river keeps only residual flow on its way through the Bergell.
why: The Bergell runs from the Maloja pass down to Chiavenna in Italy. The Castasegna station uses a head of 730 m. The electricity works of the city of Zurich (ewz) got the water rights and have made electricity in the Bergell since 1959.

From 1955 to 1959 ewz built the Albigna dam, 115 m high and more than 2100 m above sea level. Its water drives the Löbbia station. From the Löbbia basin a tunnel takes the water of the Maira down to the Castasegna station at the border. A small station at Bondo (1962) uses the Bondasca stream. ewz says that the Albigna dam also helps to stop floods.

Below the intakes the Maira, the Albigna and the Orlegna kept almost no water for many years. Since 2015 ewz releases residual flow at the Löbbia weir. The concession runs to the end of 2039. In 2023 the people of the Bergell agreed, in a consultative vote, to aim for an early new concession for ewz.
gained: The ewz plants in the Bergell make about 440 GWh of electricity per year. The federal statistics list Löbbia (1959, 86 MW, 121 GWh), Castasegna (1959, 100 MW, 267 GWh) and the smaller stations Löbbia Forno, Lizun and Bondo.
The Albigna lake holds about 70 million m³ of water.
The water fees, taxes and new jobs of the power plants helped the valley. The commune of Vicosoprano got high water fees and taxes; tourism uses the cable car to the Albigna dam.
A small turbine at Löbbia also uses the residual flow (about 0.5 GWh per year). ewz planned to start it in December 2020.
lost: The 2007 BAFU sheets show zero residual flow in every month at three intakes. They are the Löbbia weir, the Albigna dam and the Maira intake above Casaccia. The Maira between Löbbia and Castasegna (about 14 km, measured on the map) lost most of its water.
The rules for more residual flow cost ewz about 46 GWh of production per year in Graubünden.
The rock fall from the Piz Cengalo in 2017 stopped the Bondo station. Its intake had to be rebuilt for about 11 million francs. ewz planned to restart the station in spring 2025.

title: Hinterrhein power plants (KHR): Valle di Lei to Sils
place: Avers, Ferrera, Rheinwald, Schams and Domleschg (Hinterrhein valley), with the Valle di Lei in Italy
summary: Three power stations at Ferrera, Bärenburg and Sils use the water of the Hinterrhein and the Averser Rhein three times on its way from the Valle di Lei down to Sils.
why: Studies to use the Hinterrhein started in 1911–1914, and a first project followed in 1916. From 1930 the planners wanted a very large reservoir in the Rheinwald (280 million m³), which would have drowned Splügen. The communes refused it again and again. In 1946 the Federal Council decided for the communes and rejected the appeal of the power companies.

The planners then chose the Valle di Lei on the Italian border as the main store (see the change Lago di Lei). The Kraftwerke Hinterrhein company (KHR) was founded in December 1956 with Swiss and Italian partners. From 1956 to 1963 the company built 59 km of tunnels and shafts, five dams, 13 stream intakes and three power stations. At the peak in 1959, 3390 men worked on the sites, about 80 percent of them Italians on the Swiss sites.

The water is used in three steps. It goes from the Lago di Lei to Ferrera, from the Sufers reservoir (see the change Sufnersee) to Bärenburg, and from Bärenburg to Sils. Below the intakes, the Averser Rhein and the Hinterrhein now carry only residual flow (the water that must stay in the river). In 2012 the canton ordered fixed residual flows. Measures against hydropeaking (fast changes of flow below power stations) must be done by 2030.
gained: KHR has 650 MW of turbine power and 90 MW of pump power. On average it makes about 1500 GWh of electricity per year. The canton says this is almost one fifth of the hydropower of Graubünden; it is about 4 percent of the Swiss hydropower production.
The federal statistics list Ferrera (1962, 180 MW, 304 GWh per year), Bärenburg (1962, 221 MW, 475 GWh) and Sils (1961, 250 MW, 599 GWh). Ferrera also has pumps with 90 MW of power.
The building work made about 37 km of new roads and paths. The 14 concession communes get 2.8 million kWh of free electricity each year. KHR pays for the power supply to their houses.
The plant also makes single-phase current that can cover about 40 percent of the traction power of the Rhaetian Railway.
lost: Below the Sufers dam, the Hinterrhein in the Rofla gorge keeps only 0.2 to 1.5 m³/s. Before, it had from about 1 m³/s in winter to about 30 m³/s in summer (BAFU sheet of 2007).
Below Bärenburg the Hinterrhein flows through the Viamala gorge to Sils. There it keeps 0.6 to 3.5 m³/s of a summer flow of about 40 to 64 m³/s (BAFU sheet of 2007).
At Juppa in the upper Avers valley the 2007 sheet shows no residual flow. All the water of the Averser Rhein at this intake goes to the Lago di Lei.
The water from the stations at Sils and Rothenbrunnen causes hydropeaking in the Hinterrhein below Sils. Young fish and insect larvae can be stranded when the water level falls fast.

title: Blenio hydropower scheme (Ofible)
place: Valle di Blenio, from the Luzzone dam to Biasca
summary: The Luzzone and Malvaglia reservoirs and the stations of Olivone and Biasca use the water of the whole Blenio valley; the Brenno keeps only a residual flow down to Biasca.
why: The Ticino parliament gave the water rights of the Valle di Blenio in 1953. Ofible (Officine Idroelettriche di Blenio) was founded in 1956 and built its chain of plants from 1956 to 1963.

Intakes catch the Brenno and its side streams. The water goes to the Luzzone lake, then to the Olivone station, to the Malvaglia basin and to the large station at Biasca. The head from the highest basin to Biasca is more than 1400 m. The Luzzone lake is a separate change.

The Brenno flows through floodplains of national importance near Castro. Scientists studied how much water they need (1998–2005). The canton ordered more water in 2018, but the court annulled the order in 2022.
gained: Ofible's plants have 436 MW and produce over 850 GWh per year; Ofible is the second largest hydropower producer in Ticino. Ofible's own website gives 400 MW and 835 GWh. The federal list gives Biasca 327 MW and 631 GWh, Olivone 110 MW and 207 GWh.
The new roads to Campo Blenio and into the Val Malvaglia opened in the 1950s. They were built for the Luzzone and Malvaglia reservoirs, says the HLS.
The canton pays 30 percent of the water fees (money the power companies pay for the water) to the communes.
lost: The official sheet for the Luzzone intake gives no residual flow (0 l/s). At the intake TI-025 on the Brenno della Greina, 100 to 300 l/s must stay in the stream, while the flow above the intake is 0.6 to 2.6 m³/s.
The floodplains of the Brenno near Castro are of national importance. Experts said a floodplain needs 40 to 50 percent of its natural mean summer flow to keep working.
Below the sewage plant of Olivone the Brenno has too little water for the required water quality, says the canton. Bathing limits for bacteria are generally exceeded in the main Brenno.
The canton ordered higher flows in 2018. Ofima and Ofible went to court, and in April 2022 the court annulled the order.

title: Linth-Limmern hydropower scheme (Tierfehd, Linthal, Limmern pumped storage)
place: Upper Linth valley (Glarus Süd): Limmernsee, Muttsee, Tierfehd and Linthal
length_km: c. 9.5 (dry stretches of the Linth and the Limmerenbach)
summary: The Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern collect the streams at the head of the Linth valley in the Limmernsee and use the water in stations at Tierfehd and Linthal; since 2016 a 1000 MW pumped storage plant in the mountain links the Limmernsee with the Muttsee.
why: From 1957 to 1965 the company Kraftwerke Linth-Limmern built a high-pressure storage scheme at the head of the Linth valley. The Limmern dam closed the Limmernboden (see the change on the Limmernsee). Many streams around Tierfehd were caught in tunnels.
The water drops more than 1000 m to the stations at Tierfehd and is used again at Linthal. From the compensation basin at Linthal it goes back into the Linth.

In 2005 the operator Axpo presented the project 'Linthal 2015'. Building started in 2009. The new pumped storage plant (it pumps water up when power is cheap and makes power when it is needed) lies in a cavern near the Limmern dam. It pumps water 630 m up into the Muttsee. It went into service in 2016/17.
gained: The stations Tierfehd (Limmern and Hintersand stages) and Linthal have together about 386 MW and an expected production of about 540 GWh per year.
The Limmern pumped storage plant has 1000 MW in turbine and in pump mode. It raised the power of the scheme from about 520 MW to 1520 MW and cost 2.1 billion francs.
The scheme of 1957–1965 brought about 40 jobs, tax income for Linthal and water fees for the local communities (Tagwen). Building the pumped storage plant employed well over 3000 workers.
lost: The Limmerenbach below the Limmern dam gets no minimum flow (0 l/s on the official intake sheet).
At the Tierfehd intake the Linth keeps 600 l/s from April to October and no water from November to March (official intake sheet). The Linth down to Linthal is a residual flow stretch.

Below Linthal the plant causes hydropeaking over 30 km down to the Walensee. From 2006 to 2011 the high flow was 16 to 32 times the low flow; a canton study says biological indicators were very probably harmed.
Pumped storage uses more electricity than it gives back: the WWF says Linthal 2015 uses 25% more power for pumping than it produces at peak times.

title: Vorderrhein power plants (KVR): Curnera, Nalps, Santa Maria, Sedrun and Tavanasa
place: Upper Surselva: Tujetsch, Medel, Disentis, Sumvitg and Breil/Brigels
summary: Three reservoirs in the side valleys of the upper Vorderrhein feed the power stations of Sedrun and Tavanasa; the Vorderrhein and its side streams keep only residual flow below the intakes.
why: The Kraftwerke Vorderrhein (KVR) use the water of the upper Vorderrhein and its side valleys, a catchment area of about 316 km² down to Tavanasa. The reservoirs store water for electricity in winter and at peak hours.

The three dams were built between 1958 and 1968, says the Swiss dam committee: Nalps (1958–1962, 127 m high), Curnera (1962–1966, 153 m) and Santa Maria (1964–1968, 117 m). The operator Axpo gives 1962–1968 for the reservoirs. Curnera and Nalps lie in uninhabited side valleys. The Santa Maria lake at the Lukmanier pass took the place of the old hospice and chapel in 1964. Both were built again on the pass road; the new hospice opened in 1965.

The water goes first to the Sedrun station. Then a tunnel takes it to a basin at Runcahez near Sumvitg and on to the Tavanasa station. So the Vorderrhein between Sedrun and Tavanasa and the streams below the dams carry only residual flow. The water rights end in 2048.
gained: The federal statistics list Sedrun (1968, 150 MW, 246 GWh per year) and Tavanasa (1962, 180 MW, 560 GWh per year). Together they give 331 MW of peak power.
The three lakes store about 153 million m³ of water: Santa Maria 67, Nalps 44.5 and Curnera 40.8 million m³.
The canton of Graubünden (10 percent) and the concession communes (8.5 percent) own part of the company. The commune of Medel lives in part on water fees, among others from the Santa Maria lake.
A small 2.5 MW power station now works in the tunnel between Curnera and Nalps (Axpo, 2022). Before, this tunnel only moved water. The station makes up to 10 GWh per year.
lost: Below the Sedrun intake the Vorderrhein loses most of its water down to Tavanasa, about 26 km of river (measured on the map). The natural flow at the intake is about 0.4 m³/s in winter and about 5 m³/s in June (BAFU sheet of 2007).
Four side streams also keep only residual flow below the dams and intakes. They are the Rein da Medel, the Rein da Curnera, the Rein da Nalps and the Rein da Sumvitg.
The Santa Maria lake flooded the old hospice and chapel at the Lukmanier pass. The abbey of Disentis had built the hospice in 1374.
The lakes of Nalps, Curnera and Santa Maria covered three high alpine valley floors (91, 82 and 177 ha of lake surface).

title: Mattmark network: the Saas valley to Stalden
place: Saastal (Mattmark, Saas-Almagell, Saas-Grund) and Stalden
built: c. 1960–1967 (stations from 1965 and 1966; full use from 1969)
summary: The water of the Mattmark lake and of the Saas side streams falls in two steps to Zermeiggern and Stalden; the official sheets list no residual flow release on the Saaser Vispa below the dam.
why: Kraftwerke Mattmark AG built an earth dam at Mattmark (see the change 'Mattmark'). The federal dam register lists it as an earth dam of 117 m, in service since 1967.

Intakes on the Allalin glacier stream, the Hohlaubbach, the Furggbach, the Almagellerbach and other streams feed the scheme. The first step goes from the lake to the Zermeiggern station at Saas-Almagell. At Zermeiggern a second intake takes the Saaser Vispa again and leads it through a tunnel to Stalden. The water returns to the Vispa at Stalden.

In 2025 the operator began to study raising the dam by 10 m. The lake would hold about 18% more water, and about 60 GWh would move from summer to winter. This needs an extra concession and an agreement with the eleven concession communes and the canton.
gained: The federal statistics list Stalden with 185 MW and 527 GWh per year (from 1965) and Zermeiggern with 74 MW and 133 GWh (from 1966).
The ten-year average production was 647 million kWh in 2015. The towns of Sion and Sierre are among the owners.
lost: At the dam, the official sheet shows that all the water is taken: the flow taken equals the flow above the intake in every month.
At Zermeiggern, the official sheet for the Saaser Vispa (Stalden intake) also shows all the water taken in every month.

title: Verzasca hydropower scheme (Verzasca SA)
place: Lower Valle Verzasca, from the Contra dam to Tenero
summary: The Contra dam sends almost all the water of the Verzasca to the Gordola station; a fixed residual flow of 1 m³/s is released only further down, at the Tenero station.
why: Verzasca SA uses the water of the Verzasca. From 1961 to 1965 it built the Contra dam and the Gordola station at its foot. The Lago di Vogorno is a separate change.
The used water goes back into Lago Maggiore west of Tenero (official return point). The last part of the river, through the gorge and past Tenero, lost most of its water.
Since 1972 a small station at Tenero produces electricity from the residual flow (the water that must stay in the river).
gained: The Gordola station has 114 MW and produces about 215 GWh per year. The residual flow station of Tenero (1972) adds 4.25 MW and about 16 GWh.
The residual flow goes through a turbine, so Verzasca SA loses no production. It loses only money, because the station must run all the time.
lost: Above the intake the Verzasca carries on average (official sheet) 2.6 m³/s in January and 29.9 m³/s in May. The official residual flow is 1 m³/s, all year.

The 1 m³/s is not released at the dam but at the Tenero station further down, says the official sheet. The canton says that no water is released at the intake. The gorge between the dam and the Tenero station may therefore get very little water; this was not checked on site.
The canton calls the river below the dam monotonous: gravel and stones move only in big floods. The transport of bed material is strongly changed.

title: Engadin power plants (EKW): Livigno, Ova Spin, Pradella and Martina
place: Engadin: Inn from S-chanf to Martina, and the Spöl from Punt dal Gall through the Swiss National Park to Zernez
summary: Three power stages use the Spöl and the Inn from the Lago di Livigno down to the Austrian border; the Inn below S-chanf and the Spöl in the National Park keep only residual flow.
why: The Engadiner Kraftwerke company (EKW) has worked since 1954 on the use of the Inn and the Spöl. The Spöl touches the border with Italy and flows into the Swiss National Park below the Punt dal Gall dam. So Switzerland and Italy made a treaty on its water. On 7 December 1958 Swiss voters accepted the Spöl treaty with 75 percent yes.

In 1962 the Confederation gave EKW the concession for the Spöl. EKW built the Punt dal Gall dam (see the change Spöl) and four long tunnels. They go from Punt dal Gall to Ova Spin (8 km), from S-chanf to Ova Spin (15 km), from Ova Spin to Pradella (20 km) and from Pradella to Martina (14 km). Ten intakes take water from the rivers. The stations at Ova Spin and Pradella started in 1970, the Martina station in 1994.

The concession asked for a residual flow of 1 m³/s on average in the Spöl. Since 2000 two or three artificial floods per year move the gravel again. In 2011 the Confederation set the residual flow of the Spöl. In 2015 EKW added residual flow at the Clemgia and Vallember intakes.
gained: EKW makes about 1390 GWh of electricity per year, about 3 percent of Swiss consumption (EKW, 2014). The federal statistics list Ova Spin (1970, 52 MW, 89 GWh, with 47 MW of pumps), Pradella (1970, 288 MW, 969 GWh) and Martina (1994, 80 MW, 282 GWh).
The owners are Alpiq, Axpo, BKW, CKW, the canton of Graubünden and the concession communes. EKW has about 50 employees (66 in 2014) and trains apprentices in the Engadin.
The artificial floods in the Spöl since 2000 started natural processes again, such as bank erosion and river dynamics.
lost: At S-chanf the Inn keeps 0.8 to 3 m³/s. Its natural flow there is about 4 m³/s in winter and up to 58 m³/s in June (BAFU sheet of 2007). The Inn from S-chanf to Martina (about 61 km, measured on the map) carries much less water than before.
Below the Punt dal Gall dam the Spöl in the National Park keeps 0.55 to 1.45 m³/s. Before, it had up to about 12 m³/s in summer (BAFU sheet of 2007).
Below intakes, dams and stations the water level can rise suddenly. EKW warns people not to stay on the banks of the Inn below S-chanf and of the Spöl.
The Clemgia and the Vallember got residual flow only in 2015, more than 40 years after the works.

title: Hongrin–Léman pumped storage scheme (Lac de l'Hongrin to Veytaux)
place: Vaud Prealps: Lac de l'Hongrin above Montbovon, water tunnels to Veytaux on Lake Geneva
summary: The Forces Motrices Hongrin-Léman dammed the Hongrin in the Prealps and linked the reservoir with Lake Geneva, 880 m lower, so water can be turbined down or pumped up.
why: Engineers studied how to use the drop between the Grand-Hongrin and Lake Geneva for electricity. The plan was a large pumped storage plant (it pumps water up when power is cheap and makes power when it is needed), to work together with future nuclear power stations. The cantons of Fribourg and Vaud signed an agreement in 1958, but the concession was delayed because some communes of the Intyamon (upper Sarine valley) opposed it.

Work at the dam site began in autumn 1963. Two arch dams were concreted from 1966 to 1967. The power station was dug into the rock at Veytaux near Chillon from 1965. More than 20 km of tunnels bring water from eight intakes in the neighbouring valleys. The scheme went into partial service in 1970 and was inaugurated on 21 April 1972.

In 2007 the owners decided to double the power with a second station, Veytaux II. It was built from 2011 and went into service in 2017. Most water of the Hongrin at the dam now goes to Veytaux; an artificial flood once a year is meant to bring back some river dynamics below the dam.
gained: Veytaux I and II have 480 MW installed power. WASTA lists 420 MW in turbine mode (60 MW are kept in reserve), 480 MW pump power and an expected production of 162.5 GWh per year from natural inflow.
The two dams hold 52 million m³ of water. This is about 100 GWh of energy, or about 10 days of the electricity use of the canton of Vaud.
The operator says pumped storage helps to keep the Swiss and European grid stable as more wind and solar power comes in.
lost: The water of the Hongrin no longer flows down to the Sarine at Montbovon; it goes through the mountain to Lake Geneva. The intakes also take water from a further 45 km² of neighbouring valleys.
Below the dam the Hongrin lost its natural changes of flow. The operator now makes an artificial flood once a year to bring back some dynamics, and the river can rise very fast.
Pumping and turbining make the level of the Lac de l'Hongrin go up and down quickly. Warning signs were set up around the lake.

title: Gebidem dam and Bitsch power station (Electra-Massa)
place: Massa gorge below the Aletsch glacier, between Naters, Riederalp and Bitsch
summary: An arch dam in the Massa gorge catches the meltwater of the Aletsch glacier and sends it 750 m down to the underground Bitsch station.
why: The Massa drains the Great Aletsch glacier. In summer it carries very much water and sediment. Its catchment is 196 km².

The Gebidem arch dam is 122 m high. Its operator Alpiq gives 1964 for the construction and 1969 for the start of service. The lake is small (9.2 million m³), so it works mainly as an intake. A tunnel and shaft take the water 750 m down to the underground Bitsch station. The water returns to the Rhône at Bitsch.
Glacier water is hard on the machines. At high flow, the turbines take 55,000 litres per second with up to 40 tonnes of sediment per hour.
gained: The Bitsch station has 340 MW. The operator gives an average of 623 GWh per year; the federal statistics expect 770 GWh.
The water rights end in 2048. Then the wet parts of the plant can return free of charge to the communes that own the water.
lost: The official sheet for the Massa at Gebidem gives a release of 0 l/s in every month. In July about 44 m³/s arrive from the glacier.
The whole Massa gorge, about 5 km (measured on the map) between the dam and the Rhône, lies below the intake.

title: Emosson network and the Nant de Drance pumped storage plant
place: Vallée du Trient, Val Ferret, Finhaut and Martigny; with intakes in the upper Arve valley (France)
summary: Tunnels bring water from the Val Ferret, the Trient valley and French glaciers to the Lac d'Emosson; since 2022 the Nant de Drance plant pumps water up and down between two lakes.
why: In the 1950s a plan grew to build a much larger dam on the Barberine plateau. It would collect the waters of nearby valleys in France and Switzerland and drown the SBB dam of 1925 (see the change 'Emosson'). The SBB and the Emosson company agreed in 1961. Switzerland and France signed a convention in 1963. The federal concession of 1966 runs until 31 December 2055.

The concession allows the company to collect the water of the upper Val Ferret, the Saleina, the Val d'Arpette, the Trient and other streams at about 1,520–1,575 m. The water flows to the Les Esserts compensation basin and is pumped up to Emosson. Water from the upper Arve, Giffre and Eau Noire basins in France flows to Emosson by gravity. The water is used at Châtelard, Les Esserts and La Bâtiaz down to the Rhône at about 453 m.

Works for Nant de Drance began in 2008. In 2011 the owners decided to raise the power from 600 to 900 MW. The Vieux Emosson dam was raised (finished 2014). The plant lies 600 m underground and went into service in 2022. It pumps water from Emosson up to Vieux Emosson and lets it down again to make power. The operator says this helps the security of supply.
gained: The federal plant statistics list Châtelard-Vallorcine with 280 MW and 427 GWh per year and La Bâtiaz with 190 MW and 435 GWh per year (both from 1978).
Nant de Drance has 900 MW and can store 20 GWh. It changes from full pumping to full power in 5 minutes, with an efficiency of over 80%.
Building Nant de Drance took 14 years, more than CHF 2 billion, 18 km of tunnels and up to 650 workers.
lost: The official sheet for the Trient intake gives a release of 0 l/s in every month.
At the Torrent de la Fouly in the Val Ferret, the official sheet gives a release of 350 l/s only from June to September, and 0 l/s in the other months.
Water from glaciers in the upper Arve basin in France no longer flows to the Arve. It is led to Emosson and reaches the Rhône in Valais.

title: Sarganserland power plants (KSL): Gigerwald, Mapragg and Sarelli
place: Calfeisental, Taminatal and Weisstannental, with the Sarelli station on the Rhine near Bad Ragaz
summary: The Gigerwald reservoir collects water from the Calfeisental and the Weisstannental; a pumped storage station at Mapragg and a second station at Sarelli use it, and the Tamina and the upper Seez keep only residual flow.
why: The Kraftwerke Sarganserland company (KSL) built a storage scheme in the mountains above Bad Ragaz. The Gigerwald dam (see the change Gigerwaldsee) was built from 1973 to 1975, the Mapragg dam from 1972 to 1973. Operation started in 1976; the federal statistics give 1977 for Mapragg and 1978 for Sarelli.

A tunnel brings water from the Seez and its side streams in the Weisstannental into the Gigerwald lake. From the lake up to 74 m³/s go to the Mapragg station. Mapragg can also pump up to 36 m³/s back into the lake. From the Mapragg basin the water goes to the second station, Sarelli.
So the Tamina below Gigerwald and below Mapragg, and the Seez below its intake, keep only residual flow. The water rights end in 2057.
gained: The federal statistics list Mapragg (1977, 280 MW, 177 GWh per year, with 162 MW of pumps) and Sarelli (1978, 90 MW, 180 GWh per year).
Mapragg is a pumped storage station: it can pump water back up into the Gigerwald lake and use it again later.
The Gigerwald lake stores about 33 million m³ of water from a catchment of 97 km².
lost: On the 2007 BAFU sheet the residual flow of the Tamina at the Gigerwald dam was zero in every month.
Below the Mapragg basin the Tamina keeps 2.5 m³/s all year (BAFU sheet of 2007). It flows through the Tamina gorge to Bad Ragaz.
The Seez in the Weisstannental keeps 150 l/s below the intake (BAFU sheet of 2007). The rest of its water goes into another valley, the Calfeisental.

title: Hydropeaking: rivers that rise and fall every day
place: Rivers below about 100 storage power stations, mainly in the Alps; examples: Aare at Innertkirchen, Doubs
built: Problem since the large storage plants (mainly 1950–1970); law of 2009 (in force 2011); remediation deadline 2030
summary: Storage power plants release much water when electricity is needed and little at other times; since 2011 the law requires that serious hydropeaking is reduced and fish migration restored by 2030.
why: Storage power stations use much water when demand for electricity is high. They return it to the river, and the flow rises fast (Schwall, surge). When demand is low, the flow falls again (Sunk, drop). The flow can rise to many times its size within minutes. Fish and small animals strand when the water falls.

In 2006 the Swiss fishing association handed in the popular initiative 'Living water' (Lebendiges Wasser). It asked, among other things, to reduce the damage from hydropeaking. Parliament changed the water protection law on 11 December 2009 as a counter-proposal. The initiative was withdrawn in 2010, and the new rules came into force in 2011.

The law says that operators must prevent or remove hydropeaking that seriously harms native animals, plants and their habitats (Art. 39a). Plants that block fish migration or disturb the gravel flow must also be remediated. All this must be done by 2030. The operators get 100% of the costs back from a fund; electricity users pay 0.1 cent per kWh into it.
gained: In 2014 the cantons listed about 100 hydropower plants that must reduce hydropeaking, and about 1,000 obstacles at hydropower plants that block fish migration. The work must be finished by 2030.
On the Doubs, a new water rule of 2017 coordinates three power plants and reduces the flow changes on more than 40 km. Between 2004 and 2020 the number of fish doubled on average.

At Innertkirchen the Oberhasli company (KWO) built a basin of about 20,000 m³ (80,000 m³ with the tunnel). It returns the water slowly to the Aare. A regional magazine calls it the largest hydropeaking basin in Switzerland.
By the end of 2023, about 470 million francs had been promised for remediation projects, of which 176 million for hydropeaking.
lost: Remediation is slow. At the end of 2022 only 4 of 107 hydropeaking plants were fully remediated; for 26 plants the work had not started.
Some measures help only in part. The KWO ecologist says the Hasliaare lacks shallow gravel banks where young fish can hide.
The measures cost money. In 2006 the BFE said that measures against hydropeaking could reduce the profit of hydropower.

notes: A text-only change with places only: no river stretch with hydropeaking is drawn, because no official national layer of hydropeaking stretches was used. Places are WASTA power stations (state 31.12.2025). The Innertkirchen basin lies below the meeting of the Gadmerwasser and the Hasliaare (EPFL model study); its point is shown at the station Innertkirchen 1, not at the exact basin. The opening year of the basin was not found in a primary source; the KWO magazine Grimselstrom (27 August 2016, an interested party) describes it as built and in use. The Doubs example and all numbers are from the BAFU report of 25 September 2024 (state end of 2022). The Doubs plants are Le Châtelot (CH/F), Le Refrain (F) and La Goule (CH/F); La Goule was not found by name in the WASTA query and is not shown. Law date 11 December 2009 and the withdrawal of the initiative are from the Federal Gazette notices of 2 February and 22 June 2010. Map years: 1970 (end of the great building time), 2011 (new law). Sources check: quotes re-checked in opened sources (BAFU report 2024, BFE Exkurs 2006, BBl 2010 4157, gr.ch ANU page, Plattform J, WASTA). Removed claims not found as stated: 'at night, on weekends and on holidays', 'much more often and faster than a natural flood', 'washed away when it rises', 'built from 1950 to 1970'. Summary: 'requires the cantons' changed to the law's wording (operators remediate, by 2030). In-force date 1 January 2011 sourced from gr.ch. EPFL ref replaced by Plattform J (both basin volumes there). 'Largest basin' now attributed to Plattform J, not KWO.
